opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that human data only really works if you close the embodiment gap from both sides. People tend to focus on the learning side, how do we retarget human motion, how do we learn better representations, but a lot of the problem is actually at the hardware and control level.

The first thing is the end effector. Human hands do an enormous amount of the work in manipulation, and if your robot has a parallel-jaw gripper, a huge fraction of what humans demonstrate just doesn't transfer. You can't learn in-hand reorientation or a lot of contact-rich behavior from watching people if the robot physically can't express it. So I think we need hands, or at least end effectors, that are expressive enough to capture the important modes of human manipulation. They don't have to be anatomically perfect, but they need to cover the same space of useful behaviors.

The second thing is compliance and force control. Humans are incredibly compliant. When you wipe a table or insert a plug, you're not tracking a precise trajectory, you're regulating contact. If the robot is a stiff position-controlled arm, then even if you perfectly extract the kinematics from a human video, executing them will be brittle. A small error means you either miss the object or you push too hard. So robots need low-level controllers, impedance control, torque sensing, back-drivable actuators, that let them absorb the mismatch between what the human did and what the robot can do.

Third is sensing. A lot of what humans rely on isn't visible in video: tactile feedback, force, proprioception. If we want human data to carry that information, we need to capture it on the human side with gloves or wearable sensors, and have matching sensing on the robot so the policy is conditioned on the same kinds of signals. Otherwise you're asking the model to infer something it fundamentally can't observe.

And finally, I think the control interface matters a lot. If the policy outputs something like end-effector poses or keypoints, which are more embodiment-agnostic, and then a good low-level controller handles the robot-specific details, human data becomes much more usable. That kind of hierarchical design, where the high-level intent comes from human data and the low-level execution is robot-specific and robust, is where I'm most optimistic.

So in short: expressive hands, compliant control, matched sensing, and the right abstraction between them. Get those right and human data stops being a nice add-on and becomes something you can actually scale with.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expressive end effectors, compliant control, sensing, and control abstractions, but does not say robots must execute movements at roughly human speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because there's this assumption floating around that if we just collect enough human data, the robot will figure out the rest. And I think that's only half true. The data is only as useful as the robot's ability to actually execute what the data implies.

So at the hardware level, the first thing is that the embodiment gap has to be small enough that the mapping from human motion to robot motion isn't lossy in ways that matter. If a human demonstrates something with a five-fingered hand and your robot has a parallel-jaw gripper, you're not learning from the human data, you're learning from a very aggressive retargeting of it, and a lot of the information about contact, about compliance, about how the hand conforms to the object, just gets thrown away. So I think the hardware needs to be, I'd say, morphologically compatible with how humans do things. That doesn't mean it has to be identical, but the degrees of freedom and the workspace have to overlap meaningfully.

The second thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is sensing. Humans use tactile feedback constantly, and most of our human video data doesn't capture any of it. So if your robot has no tactile sensing, you're asking it to reproduce behaviors that were generated with a whole sensory channel it doesn't have. I think good tactile sensing, and proprioception that's actually accurate, is almost a prerequisite for human data to transfer for anything contact-rich.

And then at the control level, I think the key thing is compliance. Human demonstrations are inherently compliant. When you push on a table, your arm gives a little. If your controller is a stiff position controller tracking a trajectory, then small errors in the learned policy become large forces, and things break, or the object slips, or you just fail. So having a control stack that can operate in a force or impedance space, where the policy can express something like "move this way but yield if you meet resistance," I think that's really important. It also makes the learning problem easier, because the policy doesn't have to be millimeter-accurate for the behavior to succeed.

The last piece is latency and reactivity. A lot of what makes human manipulation robust is fast, closed-loop correction. If your perception-to-action loop is running at a few hertz, you can't really do that, and you end up relying on the demonstration being open-loop reproducible, which it usually isn't.

So to summarize: compatible morphology, rich sensing especially tactile, compliant control, and a fast enough loop that the policy can actually react. If you have those, then I think human data becomes really powerful. If you don't, you end up fighting the hardware instead of learning from the data.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a fast perception-to-action loop so the robot can react, but does not state that the robot must execute movements at roughly human speed.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the robot needs to be able to execute the kinds of behaviors we’re showing it. Human data can tell you what to do, but it doesn’t automatically tell you how to control a different body. If I watch someone pick up a cup, I can infer the goal and roughly how they approach it. But the forces, the contact points, the way the fingers adapt—that depends on the hardware.

So on the hardware side, you need enough dexterity and sensing to support those interactions. On the control side, you need reliable feedback: the ability to detect contact, adjust the grasp, and recover when something slips. You can’t expect a model trained on human video to compensate for all of that by itself.

I don’t think the robot necessarily has to look exactly like a human. But it needs a way to translate human actions into behaviors its own body can reliably perform. That’s what makes human data useful beyond just recognizing what’s happening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dexterity, sensing, and reliable feedback, but does not state that robots need to execute movements at roughly human speed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the robot needs to be able to execute the kinds of behaviors we see in human data. If you watch someone manipulate an object, there’s a lot happening through contact—small adjustments in the fingers, compliance in the arm, feedback from touch. If the robot doesn’t have those capabilities, more video alone won’t close that gap.

At the hardware level, that means capable hands, useful sensing, and a body that can interact reliably with the world. It doesn’t necessarily have to look exactly like a human. But there needs to be a way to map what the human is doing onto what the robot can physically do.

And at the control level, you need a robust layer that turns a higher-level intention into actual motion. Human data might tell you where to grasp or how an object should move, but it doesn’t directly tell you the motor commands for a particular robot. The robot still needs feedback to handle the details: whether the object is slipping, whether the contact is different than expected, whether it needs to adjust. That’s what makes human data useful rather than just something the robot can imitate visually.

r001.rationale: The response discusses contact, sensing, and feedback but does not state that robots must execute movements at roughly human speed.
